title: Dryback: Measurement, Interpretation, and Limits
objective: Define dryback with explicit units and reference points, then interpret the change without turning an industry shorthand into a universal plant target.

terms.definition: Measured decline in substrate water status between defined reference times.
Difference in volumetric water content expressed as percentage points.
Change divided by a stated starting or reference value and expressed as a percent.
Change during a defined lights-off interval, with irrigation and timestamps specified.

coreScience: Dryback is not one standardized number. It may mean loss of container mass, decline in VWC percentage points, relative decline from post-irrigation peak, or movement in matric potential. A report of '20% dryback' is uninterpretable unless the numerator, denominator, units, sensor, start time, and end time are stated.

The water-content curve reflects plant uptake, surface evaporation, drainage, redistribution, substrate shrinkage, sensor location, and temperature or EC effects on the probe. Early post-irrigation decline may include free drainage, while later decline may more closely reflect crop water use. Treating both segments as one physiological response can mislead.

Larger drybacks may increase air exposure in some substrates but can also increase osmotic concentration, reduce hydraulic conductivity, and produce stress. Very small drybacks can reflect frequent irrigation, low demand, oversized containers, poor drainage, or sensor placement. Neither direction is inherently generative or reproductive.
cultivationRelevance: Define a standard curve: pre-first irrigation, each post-event peak, last irrigation, lights-off, overnight minimum, and next-day pre-irrigation. Use the same sensor positions and label drainage periods separately.

Change dryback boundaries slowly and validate with root health, substrate EC, leaf temperature, water use, growth, and final quality. Do not copy branded crop-steering percentages into a different substrate and container system.

measureAndRecord.requirement: Metric, units, start point, end point, formula, and whether change is absolute or relative.
Calibration, location, substrate, container, EC, and temperature.
Post-irrigation peak, drainage segment, daytime slope, overnight slope, and minimum.
Stage, canopy size, PPFD, VPD, cultivar, and recent pruning or stress.
Boundary rationale, change size, response period, and acceptance result.

misconceptions: Dryback is always a percentage: It may be mass, VWC percentage points, relative VWC, or matric potential.
A larger dryback automatically improves quality: Stress effects are intensity-, duration-, stage-, and genotype-dependent.
The probe trace is pure plant uptake: Drainage, evaporation, temperature, salinity, and placement also influence it.
evidenceLimits: Cannabis research does not validate universal dryback percentages for all media, containers, cultivars, and stages. Use controlled trials and publish the full measurement definition.
